1.pericope_label: A song of my wellbeloved touching his vineyard: a very fruitful hill, fenced and planted

schools.summary: Hear deliberate irony in the minstrel's opening, trace the parallels with the Song of Solomon, and argue the chapter's independence from what precedes despite the points of contact.
Explain the verse form by the need for a lasting record everyone could repeat, and refuse to read the fruitful hill as Jerusalem's situation, keeping it inside the allegory.
Solve the difficulty of author and addressee by a textual change, and turn the horn of oil into a survey of how landscape borrows the parts of animals.
Give the reasons for putting a reproof into verse and pass on Jerome's note that the wellbeloved sang this song in effect over the city.

debates.question: Why does the prophet call God his beloved, and who is addressed?

positions.view: the answer that he was a kinsman of Christ is forced; he takes the office of the bridegroom's friend, to whom the bride is entrusted
the received text makes the song's author and its addressee the same, which is avoided by reading a song of loves
the beloved is deliberately left unnamed and turns out later to be the LORD himself
the Father dictates it in honour of the Son, made lord of the vineyard
either the Father or Christ, the prophet's own people being a third and weaker candidate
the song is sung to the Lord of the vineyard and was given the prophet, not devised by him

debates.question: What does a horn, the son of oil, denote?

positions.view: a land higher than all lands as a horn stands above the body, and flowing with milk and honey; more precisely a peak standing alone, perhaps Tabor
an echo of the horn of oil used at anointings, the term being an ordinary synonym for a hill
not the situation of Jerusalem, which is unnatural and forced, but simply high ground, where vines do better
hills, being the places most commodious for vines
a very fruitful soil, the extraordinary ground of an extraordinary people

debates.question: Does this chapter stand independent of those before it?

positions.view: yes, single and alone, nearest the first chapter in subject but exceeding it in force, severity and elegance
yes, though the contacts are real and the parable grows out of an earlier verse, since a similar date proves nothing against a governing idea of its own
it is a distinct composition, perhaps the most elaborately finished in the book
its subject differs from the former, being a mirror in which the people might see their own condition

outliers.reading: Alone conjectures that the prophet drew his audience by music as well as words, appearing with harp or pipe as others had done, and alone argues that the parallels with the Song of Solomon show how early that poem was read mystically.

themes: Now will I sing to my wellbeloved a song of my beloved touching his vineyard. My wellbeloved hath a vineyard in a very fruitful hill:

2.pericope_label: What could have been done more: he looked for grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes

schools.summary: Decode each act of husbandry separately, mark where the song ends and the discourse begins, and admit the facts of the indictment while denying every excuse.
Refuse the item-by-item allegory by name, defend God's disappointed expectation against the charge of ignorance, and answer the objection that he might have turned their hearts.
Allegorise the sentence as the majority do, correct the text where the sense is destroyed, and stop on the wordplay of the closing verse.

debates.question: Should each act of husbandry be interpreted separately?

positions.view: yes: the fence is the law, the stones the old idolatries, the tower the throne of David, the winepress the temple
yes, and likewise in the sentence: the pruning is the ministers, the thorns the people's lusts, the withheld rain every blessing lost

no; the exposition that makes the fence the Spirit's protection, the tower doctrine and the stones the annoyances of error is declined, the design being simply that God did all the best householder could
the fence was wholesome laws that separated them, with a providence watchful at the yearly feasts

debates.question: What does what could have been done more admit?

positions.view: two senses: what further culture could have been given, or what remains to be done by way of punishment, ending in the ruin of the nation as state and church
it cuts off the excuse that the owner was a hard master reaping where he had not sown
not a self-reproach for wasted labour, though that reading is weighed, but the plainer question; and the objection that God might have turned their hearts is an idle evasion
the umpires are silent, and their silence indicates their consciousness of guilt

debates.question: What is made of the closing wordplay?

positions.view: Kimchi marked it, and the rabbis prized such elegance under a name of their own
a cry is not heard where every man gets what is his own, and the second table may serve as the test of the first, since where cruelty reigns religion is extinguished

outliers.reading: Alone defends God's disappointed expectation against the charge of ignorance, arguing from the song of Moses that he foreknew exactly how the people would turn out, and comparing the gospel preached to all, commanded not because obedience is expected but because the mere hearing leaves unbelievers without excuse.
Alone reports the rabbinic maxim that a scribe's duty is to set a fence about the law, and alone describes the wild grapes as sour and hard, no bigger than bilberries.

themes: And he fenced it, and gathered out the stones thereof, and planted it with the choicest vine, and built a tower in the midst of it, and also made a winepress therein: and he looked that it should bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes.
And now, O inhabitants of Jerusalem, and men of Judah, judge, I pray you, betwixt me and my vineyard.
What could have been done more to my vineyard, that I have not done in it? wherefore, when I looked that it should bring forth grapes, brought it forth wild grapes?
And now go to; I will tell you what I will do to my vineyard: I will take away the hedge thereof, and it shall be eaten up; and break down the wall thereof, and it shall be trodden down:
And I will lay it waste: it shall not be pruned, nor digged; but there shall come up briers and thorns: I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it.
For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for judgment, but behold oppression; for righteousness, but behold a cry.

8.pericope_label: Woe unto them that join house to house: ten acres of vineyard shall yield one bath

schools.summary: Read the first woe as the destruction of the old village life, supply the legal background that made family holdings inalienable, and do the arithmetic of the failed harvest.
Insist that buying a field is no sin and that only the disposition is condemned, and make the covetous themselves the blight on the fields they gather.
Correct the person of the verb, prefer Kimchi's measure of the vineyard, and state the ambition flatly as a wish to be sole owners.
Grant that the purchase is lawful and locate the fault in inordinate desire and carelessness of others, adding that if the whole earth were engrossed avarice would still thirst.

debates.question: What does the LORD speaking in the prophet's ears mean?

positions.view: not softly or secretly, since the idiom is for speaking distinctly, so that mishearing is impossible
the sentence is imperfect and a verb must be supplied from the versions
no verb stands in the Hebrew, and the abruptness may be the point
something must be supplied, God sitting as judge, but the broken oath is deliberate and holds the hearer in suspense

debates.question: How far should the covetous wish be pressed?

positions.view: to its own refutation: a man left alone could neither plough nor reap, and even the ambitious cannot enjoy renown except in a crowd
to the maxim that if the whole earth were engrossed avarice would still thirst
to the plain ambition that they alone be owners and all others their tenants
to the historical fact of smallholders expelled and a class of great proprietors risen in their place
to the syntax, the tenses reaching forward to when the land is all swallowed and no one else left in it
to the sense of the opening word, a summons on one account and a groan over punishment on another

debates.question: How is the failed harvest to be measured?

positions.view: a bath from ten acres where five hundred might be looked for, a failure like the vine blights or the Irish potato, and a tenth of the seed where thirty and a hundredfold were the rule
by Kimchi's measure, the extent ten yoke could plough in a day
as the cause of the empty houses rather than a second stroke, or as the penalty for unpaid tithes
as the work of the covetous themselves, who blight the fruits as certain creatures scorch branches with their breath

outliers.reading: Alone sets the protest beside the Roman agrarian laws that checked the growth of great estates and beside Latimer's attack on enclosure, and alone conjectures that the last year of Uzziah fell in a jubilee, which may have given the complaint its edge.

themes: Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!
In mine ears said the Lord of hosts, Of a truth many houses shall be desolate, even great and fair, without inhabitant.
Yea, ten acres of vineyard shall yield one bath, and the seed of an homer shall yield an ephah.

11.pericope_label: Woe to them that rise early for strong drink: hell hath enlarged herself and opened her mouth

schools.summary: Widen the strong drink beyond wine, treat the luxurious life as practical atheism, and see in the modern pasturing of the Holy Land a literal fulfilment of the closing verse.
Distinguish ignorance as occasion from ignorance as cause, decline the ingenious expositions of the work of God, and turn the pasture into a consolation added lest the godly faint.
Judge the passage against its parallel in Amos, identify the drink from Syrian witnesses, and prefer the Greek reading of the last verse.

debates.question: Why do the people go into captivity without knowledge?

positions.view: through an ignorance gross and voluntary, occasion and cause at once, which does not excuse them since they bring it on themselves by refusing such a teacher
they did not foresee what their conduct must come to
they gave no serious consideration to God's works or their own danger
the captivity meant is neither the northern deportation, too late for a prophecy of this date, nor the fall of Judah, but Rome
the knowledge lacking was of the judgment already hanging over them

debates.question: Who are the lambs, and who the strangers?

positions.view: lambs feeding as in their accustomed pasture, with nomad shepherds eating the waste places, fulfilled in a land now given to Arab shepherds
read lambs for strangers with the Greek, the sense being that luxurious estates become pasture
oppressed lands turned to common grazing and invaders eating the produce, though the lambs may possibly be the poor set against the fat ones
the exiles themselves, called strangers because their lands had passed to the powerful, now returning to what they had despaired of
the poor Israelites left as vinedressers, strangers only because never the owners
the flock fed by the ministers of the gospel

debates.question: What is the offence of the morning feast?

positions.view: its timing as much as its quantity, banquets at dawn shocking public feeling and running on into an evening revel
that a man should rise to luxuries instead of labour, which is contrary to the order of nature
not the rising, which is healthy, but the use made of the day
the drink itself, properly palm or date wine, on the testimony of two Syrian fathers

outliers.reading: Alone measures this passage against its parallel in Amos, who probably wrote earlier, and judges that if this is the copy it hardly equals the elegance of the original.
Alone calls the life of luxury a practical atheism whose followers never see divine order in the world, anticipating in their greed the baser sort of Epicurean.

themes: Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; that continue until night, till wine inflame them!
And the harp, and the viol, the tabret, and pipe, and wine, are in their feasts: but they regard not the work of the Lord, neither consider the operation of his hands.
Therefore my people are gone into captivity, because they have no knowledge: and their honourable men are famished, and their multitude dried up with thirst.
Therefore hell hath enlarged herself, and opened her mouth without measure: and their glory, and their multitude, and their pomp, and he that rejoiceth, shall descend into it.
And the mean man shall be brought down, and the mighty man shall be humbled, and the eyes of the lofty shall be humbled:
But the Lord of hosts shall be exalted in judgment, and God that is holy shall be sanctified in righteousness.
Then shall the lambs feed after their manner, and the waste places of the fat ones shall strangers eat.

18.pericope_label: Drawing iniquity with cords of vanity: let him make speed and hasten his work

schools.summary: Take the cords as habits harnessing men to the chariot of sin, suspect an idolatrous procession behind the image, and identify the speakers of the taunt as the free-thinkers of the day.
Make the cords the self-deceptions by which men silence conscience, and read the demand for speed as a denial of providence answered by the mark that divides two sorts of men.
Report the rabbinic and conjectural readings of the rope and then dissent from all of them for a sacrificial one, and hunt a classical parallel for the counsel that comes.
Hear in the cords a confidence that will break under stress, and in the taunt the treatment of a threatened curse as a mere flash.

debates.question: What are the cords of vanity and the cart rope?

positions.view: sin added to sin until the whole runs to enormous length, like a rope-maker's work; but truer still, the silken cords by which decked victims were led to an idol's altar
habits harnessing evil-doers to the chariot of sin, the thicker rope marking where habit becomes irresistible, perhaps with an idolatrous procession in view
the allurements and pretexts by which men silence the conscience that asks what they are doing
lying arguments, with the rope as an image of effort
a false confidence, since the cords will prove vanity and break under stress; though some make the thing dragged not the sin but its punishment

debates.question: In what spirit is the demand for speed made?

positions.view: in scorn, by free-thinkers who doubted the day would come, which is to be distinguished from places where the same demand rises from impatience and weak faith
in the very words of wealthy scoffers, with a sneer at the divine title the prophet dwelt on
in a denial of providence like that of Epicurus, who thought the highest happiness lay in having nothing to do
as the inference of men who took delay for disproof

outliers.reading: Alone dissents from both the rabbis and Lowth on the cords, proposing instead the gilded horns and hoofs and garlanded heads of sacrificial victims, so that pride had the upper hand in the very acts of humiliation; and alone finds in a late Greek poet the uncommon phrase that the counsel of Jupiter was come.

Alone gives the mechanism of self-deception, that conscience quietly asks a man what he is doing and sin never advances so freely as not to feel that check, God having provided it so all should not break out into unbridled licence.

themes: Woe unto them that draw iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as it were with a cart rope:
That say, Let him make speed, and hasten his work, that we may see it: and let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel draw nigh and come, that we may know it!

20.pericope_label: Woe unto them that call evil good: their root shall be rottenness, and their blossom go up as dust

schools.summary: Set the moral confusion beside a classical historian's account of party spirit, read the woes as a chain, and take the trembling hills for a judgment still to come.
Refuse to confine the woe to judges, defend the naming of bribes against the objection that other things corrupt a bench, and read the trembling hills as punishments already endured.
Refer the shaking to the earthquake of Uzziah's reign, and make the tongue of fire the occasion for a survey of the metaphor in the poets.

debates.question: Are the trembling hills past or future?

positions.view: past: the great earthquake in Uzziah's reign, remembered as an era by later prophets
past: the shock was still fresh in men's minds
future: the verbs after therefore are prophetic preterites, so the judgment is complete and still to come
past, though the past tense often stands for the future; punishments already endured, with heavier ones ahead
the anger is kindled against a professing people, which aggravates both their sin and his indignation

debates.question: How wide is the woe on calling evil good?

positions.view: general, against the view that confines it to judges
as wide as the moral pairs are related, what is hostile to God being dark by nature and what is sweet to the taste bitter to whatever in man is godlike
as wide as history, the same inversion appearing wherever party spirit or unbelief prevails
as wide as both halves of the offence, justifying wicked men and condemning the righteous

debates.question: Do bribes alone pervert a bench?

positions.view: no, since favour and hatred blind too, but the prophet named what happens most often, and teachers should attack above all the vices custom has sanctioned
the drinkers of the earlier woe are here identified with the corrupt rulers, heroes only in and for their cups
they are renowned not for deciding guilt but for mixing strong wines, which were not properly wine but an artificial preparation
their valour belongs to the warfare of Bacchus rather than of Mars
the fire and the rotted root mark where the mirth of unjust judges ends

outliers.reading: Alone turns the tongue of fire into a survey of the metaphor, wondering that so obvious an image has not been used oftener, producing the flame that played about a boy's head in Virgil and the volcano that licks the stars, and pressing the figure to fire eating what it meets as an animal takes prey with its tongue.

themes: Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness; that put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter!
Woe unto them that are wise in their own eyes, and prudent in their own sight!
Woe unto them that are mighty to drink wine, and men of strength to mingle strong drink:
Which justify the wicked for reward, and take away the righteousness of the righteous from him!

Therefore as the fire devoureth the stubble, and the flame consumeth the chaff, so their root shall be as rottenness, and their blossom shall go up as dust: because they have cast away the law of the Lord of hosts, and despised the word of the Holy One of Israel.

Therefore is the anger of the Lord kindled against his people, and he hath stretched forth his hand against them, and hath smitten them: and the hills did tremble, and their carcases were torn in the midst of the streets. For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still.

26.pericope_label: An ensign lifted to the nations: none shall be weary nor stumble among them

schools.summary: Seek the instruments in distant lands and deny that the prophecy was written after the event, take each detail of the march as military fact, and read the closing darkness as the enemy overwhelming Judah like a sea.
Name the Chaldeans, take the lion comparison morally, and close on the impossibility of escaping the hand of God.

Take the whistle from bee-keeping, accept the march as hyperbole rightly named, prove from the ancient writers that horses went unshod, and restore a fuller reading of the last verse from the versions.

debates.question: Which distant nation is summoned?

positions.view: the Romans, since the Chaldeans were one nation and near, while this empire was many nations and reached the ends of the earth
the Chaldeans
distant nations neither in Israel nor among the neighbours, with fulfilment beginning under Ahaz
the identification is left aside for the whistle, taken from the bee-keeper's practice on the authority of two Greek fathers

debates.question: Is the description of the march literal or hyperbolical?

positions.view: hyperbole, as Kimchi rightly called it, a continued exaggeration of courage that never tires and never unlaces a sandal
military fact, down to the unloosened sword-belt, the unbroken sandal-lace, and bows already trodden, which shows the enemy near
a lion's cry taken morally, these being not men moved by compassion but savage beasts, armed so that a wayward people should learn it had to do with God
the sound of a beast just seizing its prey

debates.question: What is the darkness of the last verse?

positions.view: the darkness of a tempest suggested by the sea, or perhaps an earthquake, or an eclipse, with clouds rather than heavens
sorrow, the second noun explaining the first
a deluge in which the country suffers shipwreck, with no way out on any side, since we may escape the hand of men but not the hand of God
a fuller original reading, in which they look to the heavens above as well as the earth beneath

outliers.reading: Alone proves from the silence of the Greek and Roman writers on horse medicine that shoeing with nailed iron plates is quite modern, so that a hoof's natural firmness mattered far more then than now; and alone assembles the Greek editions, the Arabic and a second-century Coptic version to restore the last verse.

themes: And he will lift up an ensign to the nations from far, and will hiss unto them from the end of the earth: and, behold, they shall come with speed swiftly:
None shall be weary nor stumble among them; none shall slumber nor sleep; neither shall the girdle of their loins be loosed, nor the latchet of their shoes be broken:
Whose arrows are sharp, and all their bows bent, their horses’ hoofs shall be counted like flint, and their wheels like a whirlwind:
Their roaring shall be like a lion, they shall roar like young lions: yea, they shall roar, and lay hold of the prey, and shall carry it away safe, and none shall deliver it.
And in that day they shall roar against them like the roaring of the sea: and if one look unto the land, behold darkness and sorrow, and the light is darkened in the heavens thereof.
